\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2024scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require fundamentally different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE but (i)~relies on surface-level matching, explicitly acknowledging it ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs,'' (ii)~evaluates only quality estimation without studying best-of-$N$ selection, and (iii)~covers a single domain with hard prompting rather than a difficulty gradient across benchmarks.
No existing work compares confidence signals from multiple families---surface-level, structural consistency, and probabilistic---for both quality estimation and sample selection in generative structured IE.

Our central finding is that consistency-based signals are effective quality estimators but poor sample selectors for structured IE.
Entity voting achieves $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC NER and exact match leads AUROC${=}0.75$, both practically useful for quality-aware routing.
Yet no signal reliably surpasses greedy decoding on best-of-$N$ selection ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
We term this the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): instance-level signals predict \textit{which inputs} are hard, not \textit{which output} is best.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. Left: consistency signals (here entity voting) predict instance-level quality---high agreement correlates with high F1 ($\rho{\approx}0.38$, AUROC${\approx}0.69$). Right: the same instance-level signal assigns identical scores to all $N$ candidates from a given input, precluding sample selection. No signal reliably surpasses greedy on either task ($p{=}0.39$ for NER logprob).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically evaluate five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting, Soft Jaccard), surface (exact match, Fleiss' $\kappa$), and model-internal (log-probability)---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.

Our contributions are as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{First multi-family comparison of confidence signals for generative IE.}
    We evaluate five signals from three families on quality estimation for NER and RE.
    Entity voting achieves the strongest $\rho{=}0.38$ while exact match leads AUROC${=}0.75$; signal rankings depend on both task complexity and evaluation metric, with structural signals leading rank correlation on complex schemas (SciERC) and surface signals leading on simpler tasks (CoNLL).

    \item \textbf{Identification of the correlation-selection gap.}
    We demonstrate a fundamental disconnect between quality estimation and sample selection in structured IE.
    Despite strong instance-level correlations ($\rho$ up to 0.38), no signal reliably surpasses greedy on either task ($p{>}0.39$, bootstrap) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom.
    This gap reflects the instance-level nature of consistency signals, which predict input difficulty rather than discriminating among individual samples.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings depend on task difficulty: exact match leads on easy tasks (CoNLL), Soft Jaccard dominates on hard tasks (SciERC), and when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17, 54\% zero F1), inflated full-set correlations collapse on the conditional set---all signals converge toward weak or non-significant correlations once the zero/non-zero boundary is removed.
    While our NER findings are validated across three datasets of varying difficulty, our RE conclusions are based on a single benchmark (SciERC) and warrant further validation.
\end{enumerate}

3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on three English IE benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} contains 551 test instances annotated for joint NER (6 types) and RE (7 types).
10	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} provides 3{,}453 test sentences with 4 entity types, where models achieve ${>}$91\% micro F1.
11	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} consists of 1{,}287 social media instances with emerging entities, used to probe method boundaries (54\% zero F1).
12	
13	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
14	Both \textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are fine-tuned with LoRA (rank$=$32, $\alpha{=}64$) for 5 epochs using LLaMA Factory under identical training procedures, ensuring cross-model comparisons reflect architectural differences rather than training confounds.
15	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary), with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments.\footnote{$N{=}16$ results for CoNLL (Qwen) and SciERC (LLaMA) are in Table~\ref{tab:robustness} (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).}
16	Quality estimation uses Spearman $\rho$ and AUROC; downstream utility uses best-of-$N$ selection F1 with exact span matching (NER) and head-tail-label matching (RE).
17	Inference uses vLLM with constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.

On the full set, structural signals dominate on SciERC while all signals converge on CoNLL. On the conditional set, EM emerges as the strongest signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$), while logprob RE collapses to near-zero ($\rho{=}0.011$).}

58	Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} presents rank correlation ($\rho$) and AUROC for five confidence signals across tasks and models.
59	
60	\paragraph{Structural signals dominate on complex schemas.}
61	On SciERC NER, Voting achieves $\rho{=}0.379$ and SJ $\rho{=}0.360$, both outperforming surface ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and logprob ($\rho{=}0.205$).
62	The structural advantage persists on RE (Voting $\rho{=}0.350$), though all signals weaken due to the 44\% zero-F1 floor effect.
63	Entity voting and SJ show moderate instance-level correlation (NER: $\rho{=}0.659$; RE: $\rho{=}0.605$), indicating information overlap but not redundancy; their differential behavior across difficulty levels reflects the complementary granularity of entity-level frequency vs.\ span-level set overlap.
64	While $\rho{=}0.38$ explains approximately 14\% of F1 variance, the corresponding AUROC of 0.749 indicates strong discriminative power for the binary quality/failure classification most relevant to practitioners in quality-aware routing.
65	
66	\paragraph{$\rho$--AUROC dissociation.}
67	On NER, EM leads AUROC (0.749) despite ranking third in $\rho$ (0.295); on RE, EM achieves the highest AUROC (0.706) while ranking last in $\rho$ (0.134).
68	Binary agreement provides clean separation between reliable and unreliable instances, while structural signals capture finer-grained quality variation.
69	On CoNLL with LLaMA, logprob achieves the highest AUROC (0.761) yet the lowest $\rho$ (0.307), confirming this dissociation across datasets.
70	
71	\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
72	On CoNLL (greedy F1${>}$0.91), EM leads ($\rho{=}0.451$, AUROC${=}0.816$), surpassing SJ and Voting.
73	When most samples are near-correct, binary agreement captures remaining variance more efficiently than set-level similarity.
74	This reversal---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates that optimal signal choice depends on task difficulty.
75	Cross-model stability is strong: SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.436$ (Qwen) vs.\ $0.431$ (LLaMA) on CoNLL ($\Delta{=}0.005$, within 3-seed $\sigma{\approx}0.007$).
76	On WNUT-17, where 54\% of instances receive zero F1, full-set correlations are misleading: voting achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$), but this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary (conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, n.s.).
77	On the conditional set, all signals collapse toward weak or non-significant correlations ($\rho{\leq}0.35$), with SJ achieving only $\rho{=}0.089$ ($p{=}0.020$) on the full set---suggesting a capability boundary beyond which consistency signals capture binary success/failure but not quality gradation.
78	
79	\paragraph{Conditional filtering.}
80	Filtering to non-zero F1 instances reshuffles rankings (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}, right).
81	EM emerges as the strongest conditional signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$), while Voting and FK drop substantially (Voting NER: $0.379{\to}0.300$; FK NER: $0.267{\to}0.176$).
82	Logprob RE collapses to $\rho{=}0.011$, confirming its full-set correlation was driven by zero/non-zero separation.
83	This creates a natural complementarity: Voting and SJ are preferred on the full set, while EM provides the most precise ranking within the non-trivial subset (see Appendix~\ref{app:additional} for details).

118	Despite strong quality estimation, confidence signals yield limited gains when used for best-of-$N$ selection (Table~\ref{tab:selection}, Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
119	
120	\paragraph{No signal reliably surpasses greedy.}
121	We evaluate statistical significance using instance-level paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, with replacement) over $n{=}529$ NER instances, reporting 95\% percentile CIs.
122	The three random seeds (42, 123, 456) refer to independent inference runs; we average $\rho$ across seeds and report the bootstrap $p$-value of the paired difference (best signal vs.\ greedy).
123	On NER, the oracle (0.776) reveals 13.2~pp of headroom above greedy (0.644).
124	Logprob achieves the highest selection F1 (0.650, +0.6~pp), but this is not statistically significant ($p{=}0.39$; 95\% CI: [$-$3.0, +4.2]~pp; Cohen's $d{=}0.038$; sign test: 61W/70L, win\%${=}$46.6\%).
125	On RE, the gap is complete: no signal exceeds greedy (0.404) despite 18.1~pp of oracle headroom.
126	Voting ($\rho{=}0.379$, the best quality estimator) selects to only 0.634 on NER---\textit{below} greedy.

129	Instance-level confidence signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} among $N$ candidates is best.
130	When per-sample variance is low relative to instance-level difficulty, even perfect quality estimation cannot discriminate among near-identical candidates.
131	This gap has direct consequences for test-time scaling in IE \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}: closing it likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}.

135	\label{sec:robustness_main}

138	SJ NER $\rho$ shifts by only 0.028 between $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$ (bootstrap CI includes zero).
139	Doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ yields sublinear gains: SJ improves by $+0.052$ on Qwen SciERC NER, while logprob is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
140	The structural-over-logprob advantage is consistent across tested model families, holding across all four $N{=}16$ settings ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.135$ to ${+}0.175$).
141	NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}), while RE exhibits greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339).
142	For RE at $N{=}16$, SJ, FK, and logprob all plateau at $\rho{\approx}0.28$, suggesting compound errors impose a ceiling.

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
4	For per-instance quality ranking, entity voting provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$, Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}), though exact match leads binary discrimination on SciERC (AUROC${=}0.749$).
5	When temperature or cross-condition robustness is required, SJ is preferable: its temperature sensitivity is small with bootstrap CIs including zero (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}).
6	Under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$), extending binary-agreement advantages to the within-capability regime.
7	Signal rankings depend on task difficulty: EM dominates on easy tasks (CoNLL, F1${>}$0.91), Voting and SJ dominate on hard tasks (SciERC, F1$\,{\approx}\,$0.66), and when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), full-set correlations are inflated by zero/non-zero separation (Voting $\rho{=}0.724$, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, n.s.) while all signals converge toward weak or non-significant conditional correlations.
8	This ordering is consistent across tested model families, suggesting the difficulty gradient determines which signal family is most informative.
9	Conditional filtering confirms this pattern: removing zero-F1 instances shifts effective difficulty toward the easy-task regime, and EM reclaims the lead while Voting and SJ drop substantially (Voting RE: $0.350{\to}0.241$).
10	While our NER findings are validated across three datasets, our RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone and warrant further validation.
11	
12	\paragraph{Why quality estimators fail as selectors.}
13	The four instance-level signals (Voting, SJ, FK, EM) produce a single score per input, which by construction cannot rank $N$ candidates; the consensus-proximity strategy (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) converts them to per-sample scores, but the resulting selection performance (Table~\ref{tab:selection}) shows this conversion adds no reliable value.
14	Quality estimation ranks \textit{instances} by expected output quality; sample selection ranks \textit{candidates within a single instance}, requiring per-sample quality information that instance-level aggregation discards.
15	On SciERC NER, the random baseline (0.608) falls 3.6~pp below greedy (0.644), confirming per-instance sample variance exists; yet the oracle gap of 13.2~pp shows substantially better candidates exist, and the best signal captures only +0.6~pp ($p{=}0.39$).

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}
For per-instance quality ranking, entity voting provides the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$, Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}), though exact match leads binary discrimination on SciERC (AUROC${=}0.749$).
When temperature or cross-condition robustness is required, SJ is preferable: its temperature sensitivity is small with bootstrap CIs including zero (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}).
Under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$), extending binary-agreement advantages to the within-capability regime.
Signal rankings depend on task difficulty: EM dominates on easy tasks (CoNLL, F1${>}$0.91), Voting and SJ dominate on hard tasks (SciERC, F1$\,{\approx}\,$0.66), and when model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), full-set correlations are inflated by zero/non-zero separation (Voting $\rho{=}0.724$, conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, n.s.) while all signals converge toward weak or non-significant conditional correlations.
This ordering is consistent across tested model families, suggesting the difficulty gradient determines which signal family is most informative.
Conditional filtering confirms this pattern: removing zero-F1 instances shifts effective difficulty toward the easy-task regime, and EM reclaims the lead while Voting and SJ drop substantially (Voting RE: $0.350{\to}0.241$).
While our NER findings are validated across three datasets, our RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone and warrant further validation.

\paragraph{Why quality estimators fail as selectors.}
The four instance-level signals (Voting, SJ, FK, EM) produce a single score per input, which by construction cannot rank $N$ candidates; the consensus-proximity strategy (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) converts them to per-sample scores, but the resulting selection performance (Table~\ref{tab:selection}) shows this conversion adds no reliable value.
Quality estimation ranks \textit{instances} by expected output quality; sample selection ranks \textit{candidates within a single instance}, requiring per-sample quality information that instance-level aggregation discards.
On SciERC NER, the random baseline (0.608) falls 3.6~pp below greedy (0.644), confirming per-instance sample variance exists; yet the oracle gap of 13.2~pp shows substantially better candidates exist, and the best signal captures only +0.6~pp ($p{=}0.39$).
We observe a notable $\rho$--AUROC dissociation: on SciERC, EM achieves AUROC of 0.749 (NER) and 0.706 (RE) yet ranks third or last in $\rho$, because EM${=}1$ collapses both all-correct and all-wrong instances into the same binary outcome, destroying rank order while preserving discriminative power (see Appendix~\ref{app:additional} for details).
The practical implication is that these signals are well-suited for routing and triage---flagging uncertain instances for human review---but not for fine-grained ranking within a difficulty tier.

\paragraph{Why logprob fails as a selector.}
Log-probability---the sole per-sample signal---also fails at selection despite its structural advantage for candidate ranking.
Under constrained decoding, logprob primarily reflects grammar compliance rather than semantic extraction quality: a sample may have high token-level confidence yet extract the wrong relation arguments.
Bootstrap analysis reveals that 75\% of instance-level logprob comparisons are effectively ties (win\%${=}$46.6\%, comparable to random), consistent with the non-significant selection result ($p{=}0.39$).
Mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.39$; RE: $\rho{=}0.33$; Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter}), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for logprob's selection failure.
NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (ECE 0.069--0.096), but RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) suggests that logprob confidence scores are poorly aligned with extraction quality for compound tasks.
Constrained decoding enforces schema compliance at the token level, which may compress per-sample diversity beyond what free-form generation would exhibit.
The random baseline gap (3.6~pp) confirms meaningful variance exists even under constraints, but the correlation-selection gap may partially reflect this reduced diversity.
Future work should compare constrained vs.\ unconstrained decoding to disentangle these effects.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means that evaluating confidence signals on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
Effective best-of-$N$ selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} that can evaluate individual outputs rather than distribution-level properties.
Further $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:additional}) shows that $N{=}8$ captures most achievable quality estimation benefit; additional samples widen the correlation-selection gap absent stronger selectors.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

This work provides the first multi-family comparison of confidence signals for test-time scaling in generative information extraction.
By comparing five signals from three families---structural, surface, and model-internal---across NER and RE tasks of varying difficulty, we disentangle two objectives that prior work has conflated: quality estimation (ranking instances by expected performance) and sample selection (choosing the best output among $N$ candidates).
Our experiments on SciERC, CoNLL-2003, and WNUT-17 with Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B reveal that these objectives require fundamentally different signal properties.

Three findings anchor our analysis.
First, consistency-based signals are effective quality estimators: entity voting achieves the strongest rank correlation ($\rho{=}0.38$) while exact match leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.75$) on SciERC NER, with signal rankings depending on both task complexity and evaluation metric.
Second, the \textit{correlation-selection gap} shows that strong instance-level correlation does not yield substantial selection gains---no signal reliably surpasses greedy on either task (NER logprob: +0.6~pp, $p{=}0.39$; RE: $-$0.9~pp) despite 13--18~pp of oracle headroom---because instance-level signals cannot discriminate among candidates with similar consistency profiles.
Third, signal rankings depend on task difficulty: exact match leads on easy tasks, Soft Jaccard and voting lead on hard tasks, and when model capability is insufficient, inflated full-set correlations (driven by zero/non-zero separation) mask the collapse of all signals on the conditional set.
This ordering is consistent across tested model families, suggesting the difficulty gradient determines which signal family is most informative.
While our NER findings are validated across three datasets, our RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone and warrant further validation.

Several directions remain open.
Trained verifiers or reward models could close the selection gap by learning per-sample quality discrimination that unsupervised consistency signals lack.
Cross-task transfer of confidence signals beyond IE---to structured prediction tasks such as semantic parsing and code generation---would test the generality of our findings.
Integration with conformal prediction could convert continuous confidence scores into calibrated coverage guarantees.
Finally, scaling analysis with larger models (70B+) and more diverse IE tasks would clarify whether increased model capability narrows or widens the correlation-selection gap.

137	\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
138	Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}.
139	For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.052$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).

\section{Notation}\label{app:notation}

Table~\ref{tab:notation} summarizes the notation used throughout the paper.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{cl}
\toprule
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule
$\mathcal{M}$ & Language model \\
$x$ & Input instance \\
$y_i$ & $i$-th stochastic sample \\
$N$ & Number of samples \\
$T$ & Sampling temperature \\
$c(\cdot)$ & Confidence signal \\
SJ & Soft Jaccard similarity \\
FK & Fleiss' $\kappa$ \\
EM & Exact-match voting rate \\
$c_{\text{vote}}$ & Entity voting confidence \\
$c_{\text{lp}}$ & Log-probability (mean token log-likelihood) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Notation used throughout the paper.}
\label{tab:notation}
\end{table}

\section{Robustness Analysis}\label{app:robustness}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Signal robustness across configurations (Spearman $\rho$). Top: temperature on Qwen SciERC. Middle: sample size on Qwen SciERC. Bottom: cross-model transfer (LLaMA CoNLL $N{=}16$, 3-seed mean $\pm\sigma$). $^\dagger$Mean over 3 seeds ($\sigma{=}0.025$; individual: 0.428, 0.424, 0.384).}
\label{tab:robustness}
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
& & NER $\rho$ & RE $\rho$ \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\textit{Temperature} (Qwen SciERC, $N{=}8$)} \\
\quad SJ & $T{=}0.7$ & 0.388 & 0.234 \\
\quad SJ & $T{=}1.0$ & 0.360 & 0.250 \\
\quad FK & $T{=}0.7$ & 0.321 & 0.184 \\
\quad FK & $T{=}1.0$ & 0.267 & 0.275 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\textit{Sample size} (Qwen SciERC, $T{=}1.0$)} \\
\quad SJ & $N{=}8$  & 0.360 & 0.250 \\
\quad SJ & $N{=}16$ & 0.412$^\dagger$ & 0.281 \\
\quad FK & $N{=}8$  & 0.267 & 0.275 \\
\quad FK & $N{=}16$ & 0.280 & 0.279 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{l}{\textit{Cross-model} (LLaMA CoNLL, $N{=}16$, 3 seeds)} \\
\quad SJ &  & $0.463{\pm}0.007$ & --- \\
\quad FK &  & $0.455{\pm}0.006$ & --- \\
\quad EM &  & $0.460{\pm}0.008$ & --- \\
\quad Voting &  & $0.458{\pm}0.003$ & --- \\
\quad Logprob &  & $0.310{\pm}0.005$ & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_temperature_robustness}
\caption{Temperature robustness on SciERC ($N{=}8$). Top: NER; bottom: RE. SJ maintains stable $\rho$ across $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$, while FK shows mixed sensitivity. Logprob $T{=}0.7$ data unavailable.}
\label{fig:temperature_robustness}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.388 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.028 whose bootstrap confidence interval includes zero.
FK shows mixed behavior: NER $\rho$ drops by 0.054, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
Across all comparisons, the SJ--FK relative ordering is preserved at both temperatures on NER (0.388 vs.\ 0.321 at $T{=}0.7$; 0.360 vs.\ 0.267 at $T{=}1.0$), indicating a stable signal hierarchy despite numerically small temperature effects.

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.412{\pm}0.025$ (three seeds: 0.428, 0.424, 0.384), a gain of $+0.052$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent---LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$---though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.030$ (range: $+0.027$ to $+0.032$) while logprob gains only $+0.003$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is inconsistent: degradation on SciERC ($-0.007$ to $-0.019$) but improvement on CoNLL with LLaMA ($+0.027$), suggesting sensitivity to both model and task characteristics.
Voting confidence $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.062$ on Qwen SciERC), while logprob is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.021$).
SJ, EM, and voting confidence scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows setting-dependent variation, suggesting that structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.

\paragraph{Cross-model transfer.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct replicates the structural-over-surface ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.363$, FK $\rho{=}0.327$).
On CoNLL, the cross-model gap is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.
At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-logprob advantage holds across all four tested settings: Qwen SciERC (Voting $\rho{=}0.411$ vs.\ logprob 0.259, $\Delta{=}{+}0.152$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ logprob 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$), LLaMA SciERC (Voting $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ logprob 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.463{\pm}0.007$ vs.\ logprob $0.310{\pm}0.005$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.153$).

\section{Calibration Analysis}\label{app:calibration}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_reliability}
\caption{Reliability diagrams on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Top: mean F1 vs.\ binned confidence; bottom: instance counts per bin. Left: NER; right: RE. NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE shows greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), reflecting the difficulty of calibrating confidence for compound extraction tasks.}
\label{fig:reliability}
\end{figure*}

NER signals are reasonably well-calibrated (calibration ECE 0.069--0.096), while RE exhibits greater miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339), indicating that translating consistency scores into calibrated confidence estimates is feasible for NER but remains challenging for compound extraction tasks.

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives---a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over logprob remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$), indicating that longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), confirming they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: Voting reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, logprob $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$---all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for logprob's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_length_logprob_scatter}
\caption{Output length vs.\ mean log-probability on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Positive correlations (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$) rule out length-penalty confounding.}
\label{fig:length_logprob_scatter}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity.}
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ), which excludes the target sample when computing confidence, yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ, with a maximum per-instance $\Delta\rho$ of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$.
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, confirming that structural advantage is robust across both models and evaluation conditions.
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while logprob drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations---SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$)---despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set---where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs---exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2024scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.052$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals leverage $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, indicating diminishing information per additional comparison.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ logprob $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.153$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while logprob does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound---more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate---but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency decoding \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning by majority voting over chain-of-thought samples, assuming a discrete answer space.
Extensions to free-form text use LLM-based comparison \cite{chen2024usc}, atomic sub-claim decomposition \cite{thirukovalluru2024atomic}, or cross-sample hallucination detection \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
For test-time scaling, \citet{snell2024scaling} characterize compute scaling laws and \citet{brown2024monkeys} show best-of-$N$ gains across tasks.
Recent reward-free selectors include confidence-weighted voting \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc}, KL-based self-certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty}, adaptive sampling \cite{kim2026reasc}, ranked aggregation \cite{wang2025rankedvoting}, and latent-space consistency \cite{oh2025latentsc}.
Concurrently, \citet{feng2025optimal} and \citet{wang2025make} adapt self-consistency to difficulty-aware settings, echoing our finding that signal rankings shift with task complexity; \citet{li2025llms} propose generative self-aggregation for IE but focus on output fusion rather than confidence-based selection.
All of the above target reasoning/QA with discrete answers or specific aggregation strategies.
Our work extends self-consistency to set-valued structured outputs and identifies the correlation-selection gap: strong quality estimation ($\rho{=}0.38$) coexists with selection failure ($p{>}0.39$).

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{nedellec2026consistency} study consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based NER/RE, corroborating our quality-estimation findings.
However, their work differs in three key respects: (i)~it relies on surface-level matching, explicitly acknowledging it ``overlooks semantically consistent outputs''; (ii)~it evaluates only quality estimation without studying best-of-$N$ selection, leaving the correlation-selection gap unexamined; and (iii)~it covers a single domain with hard prompting rather than a difficulty gradient across benchmarks.
Our Soft Jaccard signal addresses limitation (i) through type-aware bipartite matching with token-level span overlap; our selection analysis (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}) directly addresses (ii); and our three-dataset evaluation spanning easy (CoNLL) to hard (SciERC) tasks addresses (iii).
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses model confidence with inter-sample consistency for QA/summarization but does not address structured extraction.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE work \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, josifoski2022genie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, wang2023instructuie} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and calibration.}
Several surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, selective abstention \cite{wen2025know}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and their intersection with calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic} for LLMs.
Semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic} clusters generations by meaning; \citet{kossen2024semantic} distill semantic entropy into lightweight probes; P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} queries model confidence directly; our structural signals instead measure agreement over output \textit{structure}.
Modern neural networks are often miscalibrated \cite{guo2017calibration, desai2020calibration}; our reliability diagrams extend calibration analysis to structured prediction.
Deep ensembles \cite{lakshminarayanan2017ensembles} and MC-dropout \cite{gal2016dropout} obtain uncertainty from model variation; our approach requires no model modification.
Prior NER uncertainty work \cite{xiao2019uncertainty, shelmanov2021active, zhang2023ener} operates within discriminative paradigms, inapplicable to generative settings.
Conformal prediction \cite{fisch2021conformal, angelopoulos2021conformal} provides coverage guarantees; trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify} and reward models \cite{wang2024mathshepherd} learn per-sample scoring from labeled data.
Selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective} and confidence-based IE filtering \cite{culotta2004confidence} establish the broader framework; our contribution is characterizing which signals support quality estimation vs.\ sample selection for generative IE.

\paragraph{Structural signals dominate on complex schemas.}
On SciERC NER, Voting achieves $\rho{=}0.379$ and SJ $\rho{=}0.360$, both outperforming surface ($\rho{\leq}0.295$) and logprob ($\rho{=}0.205$).
The structural advantage persists on RE (Voting $\rho{=}0.350$), though all signals weaken due to the 44\% zero-F1 floor effect.
Entity voting and SJ show moderate instance-level correlation (NER: $\rho{=}0.659$; RE: $\rho{=}0.605$), indicating information overlap but not redundancy; their differential behavior across difficulty levels reflects the complementary granularity of entity-level frequency vs.\ span-level set overlap.
While $\rho{=}0.38$ explains approximately 14\% of F1 variance, the corresponding AUROC of 0.749 indicates strong discriminative power for the binary quality/failure classification most relevant to practitioners in quality-aware routing.\footnote{For context, semantic entropy achieves AUROC $\approx$ 0.75--0.85 on discrete-answer QA tasks \cite{kuhn2023semantic}; direct comparison is complicated by the fundamentally different output spaces of structured IE versus closed-form QA.}
Bootstrap CIs for signal pair differences on SciERC NER ($N{=}8$): SJ$-$logprob $\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$ [+0.074, +0.234]; Voting$-$SJ $\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.019$ [$-$0.033, +0.073]; SJ$-$EM $\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.065$ [+0.003, +0.130].
The SJ advantage over logprob is significant, while the Voting--SJ gap is not; the SJ--EM difference is marginal (CI lower bound +0.003).

\paragraph{$\rho$--AUROC dissociation.}
On NER, EM leads AUROC (0.749) despite ranking third in $\rho$ (0.295); on RE, EM achieves the highest AUROC (0.706) while ranking last in $\rho$ (0.134).
Binary agreement provides clean separation between reliable and unreliable instances, while structural signals capture finer-grained quality variation.
On CoNLL with LLaMA, logprob achieves the highest AUROC (0.761) yet the lowest $\rho$ (0.307), confirming this dissociation across datasets.

\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
On CoNLL (greedy F1${>}$0.91), EM leads ($\rho{=}0.451$, AUROC${=}0.816$), surpassing SJ and Voting.
When most samples are near-correct, binary agreement captures remaining variance more efficiently than set-level similarity.
This reversal---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates that optimal signal choice depends on task difficulty.
Cross-model stability is strong: SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.436$ (Qwen) vs.\ $0.431$ (LLaMA) on CoNLL ($\Delta{=}0.005$, within 3-seed $\sigma{\approx}0.007$).
On WNUT-17, where 54\% of instances receive zero F1, full-set correlations are misleading: voting achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$), but this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary (conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, n.s.; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
On the conditional set, all signals collapse toward weak or non-significant correlations ($\rho{\leq}0.35$), with SJ achieving only $\rho{=}0.089$ ($p{=}0.020$) on the full set---suggesting a capability boundary beyond which consistency signals capture binary success/failure but not quality gradation.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering.}
Filtering to non-zero F1 instances reshuffles rankings (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}, right).
EM emerges as the strongest conditional signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$), while Voting and FK drop substantially (Voting NER: $0.379{\to}0.300$; FK NER: $0.267{\to}0.176$).
Logprob RE collapses to $\rho{=}0.011$, confirming its full-set correlation was driven by zero/non-zero separation.
